transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Spain is mourning the deaths of 69 people
in a high-speed train collision Wednesday south of Madrid.
Details on what caused the accident are coming in,
but NPR's Miguel Macias reports key questions remain unanswered.
At about 8.30 a.m. local time,
the main security system used in the Madrid Seville Line fell.
The backup system kicked in.
About five minutes later, a train operated by Renfé
was told to resume its transit.
First human error.
The Renfé train was told to transit at normal speed
and should have transited at about 25 miles per hour.
Minutes later, another train ahead of the first one,
operated by IDIO, was given the same instructions.
Proceed.
Minutes later, the conductor of the IDIO train
notified that she had not been able to resume transit.
Second human error.
No one alerted the Renfé train that there was a train stopped right ahead.
About five more minutes go by.
At 8.53 a.m., the Renfé train collides with the IDIO train
at an estimated speed of 120 miles per hour.
A court and a technical investigation are underway.
Miguel Macias, NPR News, Seville, Spain.
President Trump will campaign in South Carolina today
for Republican Senator Darlene Graham.
Political analyst David Wasserman is with the Cook Political Report.
He says Trump carried South Carolina by 18 points in the last election.
Darlene Graham, who was appointed to replace her brother,
has been struggling in adapting to becoming a politician.
And Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who had the airwaves to herself
for a few weeks because of a fundraising advantage,
she was able to close the gap.
Now, this race is very close, but the undecided vote here leans Republican.
So it's always going to be very difficult in a racially polarized state
for a Democrat to get to 50 percent.
He spoke to NPR's Morning Edition.
The number of students that enrolled in higher education this fall
stayed steady compared with last fall.
NPR's Alyssa Nadworney has more on the early findings
from an annual report by the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center.
For undergrads, enrollment overall is slowing.
The only sector with gains, and they were small, about one percent,
were community colleges.
This follows an increase seen in fall of 2025,
which showed college enrollment returning to pre-pandemic levels.
That gain at community college was countered by declines in enrollment
at master's degree programs.
When it comes to what students study, enrollment in computer science programs
continues to decline sharply, with double-digit decreases.
Health majors, in contrast, are growing across undergrad and graduate programs.
This preliminary report represents a little less than half of U.S. colleges
that submit their data.
A full picture will be released in January.
Alyssa Nadworney, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
National security officials have been warning for years
that Chinese government hackers might one day wreak havoc
on U.S. critical infrastructure in the event of a conflict,
such as an invasion of Taiwan.
NPR's Jenna McLaughlin reports new research shows the lengths
the Chinese government is willing to go to keep its cyber-hacking secret.
Mike Horca, a former FBI special agent,
says he watched Chinese government hackers go to great lengths
to reach key targets and hide their activities
by using previously undiscovered vulnerabilities,
hacking into a long chain of virtual networks
and compromised devices like routers
every single time they wanted to reach a new target.
It definitely felt like a wild cruise chase a lot of times.
Horca works with the Black Lotus Labs team at Lumen Technologies,
a telecommunications company that has a unique view of the flow of traffic
along the backbone of the internet.
And he says he hopes to expose the Chinese government's playbook
and shine a light on Chinese strategic priorities,
but also help defenders to shore up their systems from these kinds of attacks.
Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.
The federal government says the U.S. economy grew 3.4 percent
between July and September of this year.
The second quarter growth was stronger than the previous quarter.
At the same time, Americans are struggling with inflation
and things that are costly or just not affordable.
A separate report today says that inflation in September
accelerated 3.6 percent.
That's compared to what it was a year ago.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Spain's high-speed train collision south of Madrid kills 69 people; investigations underway
President Trump campaigns in South Carolina for Republican Senator Darlene Graham
Fall college enrollment holds steady, with community colleges up and computer science declining
Chinese government hackers hide intrusions by chaining compromised routers and devices, Lumen researchers say
U.S. economy grows 3.4 percent in third quarter, while inflation accelerates to 3.6 percent
